slides.0.title: Cognac Region and Its Six Crus
slides.0.subtitle: From Grande Champagne to Bois Ordinaires: how soil shapes style
slides.1.title: The three core crus
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Grande Champagne
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Thin clayey soils with very high limestone over soft Cretaceous chalk; fine, light eaux-de-vie with a mostly floral bouquet that need long cask ageing to mature fully (cognac.com)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Petite Champagne
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Same champagne-type chalky soils; very similar to Grande Champagne but with less finesse (cognac.com). "Champagne" here has nothing to do with the sparkling-wine region
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Borderies
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The smallest cru, on clay and flint soils from decomposed limestone; fine, round, smooth spirits with a violet aroma that peak after shorter ageing than the two Champagnes (cognac.com, Wikipedia)
slides.1.content: Hectare figures differ by source and year, so they are not tested.
slides.2.title: The outer three crus
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Fins Bois
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The largest cru, ringing the first three; red chalky clay (groies) with hard Jurassic stones gives round, faster-maturing spirits often used as a blending base (cognac.com, Wikipedia)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Bons Bois
slides.2.highlights.1.content: A large belt that includes coastal areas and the southern vineyards, on sandy soils eroded from the Massif Central (cognac.com)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Bois Ordinaires
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Along the coast and on the islands of Ré and Oléron on almost entirely sandy soil, with a maritime flavour and fast ageing (cognac.com); also called Bois à Terroir
slides.2.content: Rule of thumb: nearer the core, finer and longer-lived; further out, rounder and quicker to mature.
slides.3.title: Fine Champagne and labelling
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Fine Champagne
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Not a cru but a controlled appellation: a blend of Grande and Petite Champagne with at least 50% Grande Champagne (cognac.com, Wikipedia)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Cru designations
slides.3.highlights.1.content: A bottle naming a single cru must come entirely from it; most Cognac is blended across crus (Wikipedia)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Exam angle
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Diploma and CMS ask you to link soil (chalk to sand) with speed of maturity and style, and to define Fine Champagne
slides.3.content: The six crus date from the late 1930s; remember the order as chalk to sand.
